persona: Buyer for an online t-shirt shop

designs.title: Vitis vinifera
designs.why: Reads as a grape cluster from across the room and as a proper engraved botanical plate up close. Clean confident linework, strong tendrils, nice bud detail, legible captions. Wine-lover gift appeal is clear and it looks worth $50 on a white tee. The pruned cane sits apart on the right like a second plate, so the thumbnail looks lopsided and the main figure ends up smaller on the shirt.
designs.fix: Bring the pruned cane in closer, or tuck it under the main branch, so the composition is one tighter block. The grapevine can then print larger and fill the chest and back width better in the listing thumbnail.

designs.title: Fermentation
designs.why: Homebrew/craft-beer buyers are a proven niche, and a cutaway with Krausen, wort and yeast labels is the kind of nerdy-accurate detail they pay for. The engraving holds up at full size and works white-on-black. But the tall narrow tank makes a skinny print that looks thin and small on the tee, the small labels turn to grey specks in the thumbnail, there is a stray tick mark between the tank leg and the yeast circle (about x1700 y2925), and one yeast cell accidentally reads as a smiley face.
designs.fix: Make the layout wider: scale the tank up and let the magnified-yeast inset overlap it, so the print fills more of the shirt. Delete the stray mark and the face-like dots on that yeast cell while doing it.

designs.title: Shaping
designs.why: Surf-shop culture is a good, sellable story and the SHAPING header works as a hook. But at full size the art is a noisy threshold texture of wormy dots, not drawn lines. It reads as a filtered photo, not illustration. The face is lost under the respirator and the speckle, it looks muddy and cheap at $50, and the dense noise will fill in or crack on a one-ink print.
designs.fix: Redraw it as clean line art with deliberate hatching instead of the photo-threshold speckle. Open up the face and hands, and keep the shaped blank as the bright hero shape.
